passages.title: Email Correspondence: An Interpreter Who Did Not Arrive

emails.subject: Appointment 4 June, interpreter booked and not provided
emails.body:
Dear Patient Liaison,

I accompanied my mother to a consultant appointment on 4 June. An interpreter was booked at the referral stage and confirmed twice. No interpreter attended.

The consultant asked me to interpret. I did, because the alternative was my mother leaving without knowing her results.

I want to be precise about why that is a problem, because on the surface it looks like a solution. I am not a medical interpreter. I did not know the word for the condition in either language and I guessed. My mother then asked me a question she would not have asked a stranger, and I answered it as her daughter rather than translating it, because that is what happens when the interpreter is family. Nobody in that room can now be certain what my mother was told.

I am not asking you to discipline anyone and I do not want an apology in the abstract. I want to know two things. Whether the booking failed or the interpreter did — and whether my mother's notes record that interpretation was provided by a family member, because if they record it as an interpreted consultation then the record is wrong.

Sincerely,
Wanjiru Kamau

emails.subject: RE: Appointment 4 June, interpreter booked and not provided
emails.body:
Dear Ms Kamau,

Both of your questions have uncomfortable answers and you are entitled to them.

The booking failed. It was made against the referral and not against the appointment, and when the appointment was rescheduled in May the booking did not move with it. The agency was never told to attend on 4 June. The interpreter did nothing wrong; our system did not ask her to be there.

On the notes: they record "interpreter present". They do not record that the interpretation was provided by a family member. That is a factual error in a clinical record and I have submitted a correction, which your mother is entitled to see. I would not have found it without your email, because nothing in our process compares what was booked against what happened.

You have described the harm more clearly than our own guidance does, and I have asked for your third paragraph to be quoted in our interpreter training — with your permission, and anonymously, and I will not use it unless you say yes.

What changes: interpreter bookings now attach to the appointment rather than the referral, so a reschedule carries the booking with it. That was a configuration choice nobody had revisited.

One thing I cannot offer. I cannot tell you what your mother understood on 4 June, and neither can the consultant. She has been offered a further appointment with an interpreter present, at no charge and at a time of her choosing, which is the only remedy I can honestly describe as one.

Regards,
Tomasz Nowicki
Patient Liaison Manager

passages.title: What Happens to a Language in the Second Generation
passages.content:
The pattern by which a community language gives way to the majority language is one of the most consistent findings in the study of migration, and it is faster than most families expect. The usual sequence takes three generations: the first speaks the heritage language, the second is bilingual, and the third understands but does not speak it. What varies is not the direction but the speed, and the factors that change the speed are not the ones commonly assumed.

Parental effort is a weaker predictor than parents expect. Households that speak the heritage language exclusively at home still see substantial shift, because the decisive exposure is not at home but among peers. Children calibrate to the language of the playground, and once schooling begins the ratio of hours moves sharply. A parent competing with that ratio is competing with arithmetic.

What does predict retention is the availability of the language outside the family and outside instruction — a shop, a place of worship, a sports team, a cousin of the same age. Domains matter more than hours. A language used in one setting is a subject; a language used in four is a language. This is why community institutions correlate with retention more strongly than home policy does.

Literacy is the second strong predictor and the one most often skipped. Children who learn to read and write the heritage language retain it at markedly higher rates, because reading creates a use for the language that does not depend on other people being present. Oral-only transmission is more fragile precisely because it requires an interlocutor.

The costs of loss are usually described in cultural terms and are also practical. Families lose the ability to communicate in depth with grandparents, which affects care arrangements and the transmission of family history. There is also a documented cognitive and educational advantage to maintained bilingualism, and — a finding that surprises people — heritage-language literacy is associated with stronger rather than weaker attainment in the majority language, because the skills transfer.

The practical implication is that reversing the pattern is not mainly a matter of families trying harder. It depends on whether a child encounters the language in enough places to need it, which is a question about institutions rather than about parenting.

passages.title: Should Public Services Fund Translation and Interpreting?

viewpoints.name: Director Anneliese Brandt
viewpoints.text: We fund interpreting and the cost argument against it is the one I find easiest to answer, because it is arithmetic. An unattended interpreter costs us a wasted consultant slot, a repeat appointment and occasionally a readmission — the interpreting line is smaller than the line it prevents. The argument I find harder is the one about integration, and I will not pretend I have settled it. My honest position is that this is a safety measure and that the integration debate should be had about language teaching, where it belongs, and not about whether people can understand a diagnosis.

viewpoints.name: Yusuf Barzani, community interpreter
viewpoints.text: I am paid for the appointment, not for the waiting, the travel or the cancellation, which is why experienced interpreters leave and inexperienced ones fill the gap. The service then reports that interpreting quality is variable, which it is, and treats that as a reason to use less of it. Pay for the time the work actually takes and the quality problem substantially disappears. What is happening now is a shortage being read as a standards problem.

viewpoints.name: Dr Priya Venkataraman, health researcher
viewpoints.text: The evidence on professional interpreting is strong: better diagnostic accuracy, fewer unnecessary tests, better adherence. The evidence on the alternative is what should end the argument — using family members is associated with significant error rates, including omissions the family member makes deliberately to protect the patient. That is not a criticism of families; it is what happens when the interpreter has a relationship with the person. I would spend more, and I would spend it on removing family interpreting rather than on expanding coverage.

viewpoints.name: Councillor Fintan O'Rourke
viewpoints.text: I voted for the budget and I want to raise something the debate avoids. We fund interpreting generously and we fund English classes with waiting lists of eleven months. Those two facts sit badly together, because the first is a permanent cost and the second is the thing that reduces it. I am not proposing we cut interpreting — people need to understand a doctor today, not in eleven months. I am saying that funding only the immediate need and calling it a language policy is how the immediate need becomes permanent.
